title: The Reputation That Gets You Hired
paras: The reputation that gets you hired. A recruiter's guide to the profile, C-V and presence that make employers want you — for planners at every stage, in the U-K, in 2026.

Recruitment doesn't start when you send a C-V. After thirty years placing planners, graduate to director, I can tell you it starts long before, and never stops. By the time your application lands, someone's searched your name, read your LinkedIn, seen your appeal decisions and comments online. The C-V isn't the start — it's where a picture that already exists gets confirmed, or contradicted.

So you're not a document assessed once a decade when job-hunting. You're a reputation, built continuously, online whether you tend it or not, read before anyone speaks to you. The best jobs and fastest promotions go not to the cleverest C-V, but to the reputation that does the work before you walk in the room. One note: the recruiter figures I'll quote are from a 2025 U-K survey, with the sources in the written guide.

title: Part 1 — Building your professional brand
paras: Part one — building your professional brand. 'Brand' makes planners wince — it smells of marketing. Plainly: it's the reputation that arrives before you do, what people expect when your name comes up and you're not in the room. Not a logo, but the answer to the recruiter's quiet question: what is this person known for, and can I trust them?

And everyone already has one. The graduate who's always prepared. The senior planner known for winning difficult appeals. The officer whose reports are a pleasure to read — and the one whose turn up late and thin. A brand isn't something you have or lack; it's something you shape, or leave to chance. Most people's is an accident. Yours doesn't have to be.

First impressions form fast, and increasingly online. Around ninety-one percent of U-K recruiters use LinkedIn regularly, and about eighty-four percent screen candidates on social platforms. So your first impression isn't your handshake, or even your C-V — it's your LinkedIn photo, your headline, your last few posts, and what a search of your name throws up, judged in seconds.

And underneath it all sits trust. Recruiters place, and employers hire and promote, people they trust to do the work, represent them well, and not become a problem. Everything here — the honest C-V, the consistent presence, the clean footprint, helping colleagues — is about building that trust. A career is a long game of accumulated trust.

title: Part 2 — Writing an outstanding CV
paras: Part two — writing an outstanding C-V. It still matters — it's where your reputation gets evidenced — and it isn't hard: discipline, honesty, and avoiding a few common mistakes.

Length and layout: for almost everyone, two pages — a graduate can do one or two, only a genuinely senior planner needs a third. Keep it clean and conventional: name and contact line, a short profile, then employment in reverse order, education, qualifications, skills. A plain readable font, consistent formatting, easy on colour — one accent for headings, not a rainbow. Recruiters read hundreds; clarity beats cleverness. Send a P-D-F unless they ask for Word — it holds your formatting on any screen.

The one caveat is the applicant tracking system, the A-T-S, that many larger employers use to search C-Vs. Its U-K prevalence isn't reliably published, so treat that as uncertain — but making your C-V machine-readable costs nothing: a clean single-column layout, standard headings like 'Employment' and 'Education', no text buried in images, boxes or headers, and the keywords a search uses — chartered town planner, development management, M-R-T-P-I, Local Plan, your software. A beautiful C-V the machine can't read never reaches the human.

What goes in it: a short profile of three or four lines; employment built around achievements; education; memberships — R-T-P-I chartership, M-R-T-P-I, above all, plus R-I-C-S or I-C-E where relevant, and your C-P-D; and skills. Name the planning skills specifically — G-I-S, and which, Arc-G-I-S or Q-G-I-S; CAD; the Planning Portal and case-management systems; data analysis; and the competencies employers search for: development management, planning policy, major applications, appeals, public inquiries, committee experience, presentation. Those are the keywords recruiters search on. And the rule that matters most: achievements, not duties. A weak C-V lists what you were responsible for; a strong one shows what you did, with a result and, where you can, a number. Every planner in a role has the same duties; what sets you apart is what you achieved.

Use your own real figures, never inflated. A weak profile — 'a hardworking planner with excellent communication skills, seeking a new challenge' — could be anyone. A strong one names it: 'chartered town planner, M-R-T-P-I, seven years in development management across major residential and commercial schemes, a strong appeal record, and contentious applications steered through committee — now seeking a principal role.' Specificity is credibility.

title: Part 3 — The cover letter
paras: Part three — the cover letter. Where asked for, keep it to a page — three or four short paragraphs — doing a different job from the C-V. The C-V is the evidence; the letter is the argument, answering what the C-V can't: why this employer, and why you, for this role, now.

The structure: why them — something specific a template couldn't contain: a scheme they're on, their reputation in a sector, their growth. Then why you — the two or three things that fit, with a concrete example, not a restatement of your C-V. Then a short close: enthusiasm, availability, a confident sign-off. Never pour your C-V into prose. Never send a generic letter with the name swapped in — recruiters spot it instantly, and a wrong company name left in from the last application is a common, career-ending howler. And never make it about what you want, rather than what you offer.

The kind of thing I mean, to a firm about their regeneration scheme by name: 'I've followed your work on the scheme with real interest — strategic, contentious urban sites are where I do my best work. In four years I've taken three major residential applications to consent, one recovered at appeal, and I keep difficult schemes moving and members onside. I'd relish bringing that to your team, at four weeks' notice.' Specific, evidenced, and about them as much as you.

title: Part 4 — LinkedIn
paras: Part four — LinkedIn. For a modern professional it isn't optional — it's where recruiters and employers look first. Around ninety-one percent use it regularly, and among specialist social recruiters, effectively all of them, to search for candidates. The U-K has some thirty million users. A strong profile is a second C-V that works while you sleep — one recruiters find proactively, bringing opportunities to you.

First, be findable. Recruiters search on keywords, so your profile must contain the words they type — chartered town planner, development management, M-R-T-P-I, planning policy, your city — in your headline, about section and experience. The most wasted space is the headline, which most leave as their job title. Use it: 'Chartered Town Planner, M-R-T-P-I — Development Management and Major Applications', plus your city. And your about section should be first person: a short story carrying your achievements and keywords, reading like you, not a pasted C-V.

On the extras: recommendations are the most under-used feature and among the most persuasive — ask specifically after a job well done. Premium can help an active job-seeker, with InMail and insights; Creator mode suits regular posters; neither is necessary. And networking is being useful, not collecting contacts. Send requests with a short personal note, not the blank default — it roughly doubles acceptance. Follow who matters: the R-T-P-I, the authorities and consultancies you admire, the planning leaders you respect. And message recruiters specifically — a vague 'please find me a job' gets little; a targeted 'I'm an M-R-T-P-I development-management planner in the North West looking to move into consultancy — is that a market you work in?' gets a reply.

On posting and the 2026 algorithm — you needn't post to benefit, but a little thoughtful activity builds visibility. The algorithm shifts and no one outside LinkedIn knows it exactly, so take this as informed guidance. Consistency beats volume — two to five times a week beats a burst then silence, and a comment counts. Comments matter more than likes; the 2026 consensus is a comment's worth roughly twice a like to your reach. Dwell time and early engagement count — content people stop and read, that gets engagement in the first hour, travels furthest. And knowledge and stories perform where bait and links underperform: genuine insight, a lesson from a case, a plain-English explainer or native video, while engagement-bait and link posts get shown less.

The aim is credibility, not celebrity. Two posts that work — a reflection: 'an appeal I lost last month taught me more than any win; here's the point about heritage harm I'd underweighted.' Or an explainer: 'biodiversity net gain in ninety seconds, for anyone who still finds it baffling.' Useful, human, and clearly from someone who knows the work.

title: Part 5 — Other social media
paras: Part five — other social media. LinkedIn is the one platform that genuinely matters for a planning career. The rest run from mildly useful to actively risky, and the honest answer to 'should I be on all of them?' is a firm no — spread thin and you'll maintain none, and expose yourself on several.

So: invest in LinkedIn, keep a portfolio or blog if it suits your specialism, and treat everything else as personal space to be secured, not a career tool. The other platforms more often cost people opportunities than win them.

title: Part 6 — What employers check
paras: Part six — what employers check. They do due diligence, and you should assume they do it on you. About eighty-four percent screen candidates on social media, and around twenty-one percent have rejected someone over what they found. A typical check runs professional-outward: your LinkedIn, a search of your name, then public social media. And planners have sources most professions don't — Inspectorate decisions name the planners and advocates, so your appeal record is partly public; your R-T-P-I membership and any disciplinary record can be checked; Companies House shows directorships; and for senior hires, published papers, talks, podcasts, articles and news. For a competent professional, most of this reassures.

A word of fairness: good employers, and the professional guidance on selection, warn against over-reaching in social-media screening — it can introduce bias, stray into private life, and data-protection law applies. But you can't control where any employer draws that line, so assume anything public may be seen. The aim isn't to become bland or fearful — it's to make sure what's public is professional, or innocuous. Political views, held and expressed civilly, are your right; a stream of aggressive, offensive or extreme content is different, and it does cost people jobs.

title: Part 7 — Your digital reputation
paras: Part seven — your digital reputation. The key thing: nothing online is ever completely private, and nothing is ever completely gone. A message can be screenshotted, a 'private' group has members, a deleted post may already be captured. Old content resurfaces — photos from a decade ago, tweets you forgot, things you posted at university before you had a profession to protect. And tagged photographs put you in other people's posts, outside your control.

That's a reason for care, not panic. Do a periodic tidy-up. Search your own name and see what an employer sees. Tighten privacy so photos, posts and tags are visible to friends, not the world. Take down anything you wouldn't want a future manager, client or committee to read — not to deceive, but because youthful nonsense doesn't represent the professional you now are. Untag yourself from anything unhelpful. And apply the oldest test before you post: would I be comfortable if this appeared on the front of the local paper, next to my name, and my employer's?

What should you leave? Everything professional, thoughtful, or simply human and harmless. You're not erasing yourself or becoming a faceless corporate cipher — a real person with genuine interests is more appealing than a blank one. Clean up the risks; keep the personality.

title: Part 8 — Interview preparation
paras: Part eight — interview preparation. If your reputation and application get you to interview, preparation converts it. The planners who interview well aren't the most gifted talkers — they're the ones who prepared. Research the employer: schemes, sectors, recent news, values. Research the interviewers on LinkedIn. Anticipate the questions, often case-based — a difficult application; a refusal you defended; how you handle committee, or an angry objector; a policy point relevant to the role; why you want this job. And prepare your own thoughtful questions about the role, team and work — asking only about pay and leave does the opposite.

For competency questions, use STAR: the Situation, the Task, the Action you took — the heart of it — and the Result. So: 'a contentious sixty-home application with strong objection' — situation; 'I had to secure a recommendation members could support' — task; 'I reworked the scheme with the applicant, ran a members' briefing, and addressed the highways concern head-on' — action; 'approved with cross-party support, not appealed' — result. Far more persuasive than 'I have good negotiation skills.'

Online interviews are their own small skill. A plain, tidy background. Camera at eye level — raise the laptop — so you're not looming or looking down. Light on your face from the front, not a window behind. A decent microphone, a tested connection. Look into the camera, not your own image. And dress as you would in person — smart, erring formal.

title: Part 9 — Building a career
paras: Part nine — building a career. Getting hired is one thing; getting on is another. After thirty years watching careers, promotions rarely go to whoever served longest. They go to those who made themselves visible, valuable and trusted — who deliver, are known for something, and whom decision-makers can picture in the bigger role. Time served is the weakest career strategy; reputation is the strongest.

Employers spot future leaders by a set of signals, every one within your control. Deliver, commercially and technically. Keep your C-P-D and chartership current — the licence to progress. Develop a specialism, becoming genuinely expert in something scarce and valuable; 'the person for energy consents', or 'the one who wins the difficult appeals', has a reputation that markets itself. Build visibility — the occasional article, a talk, a committee. Network genuinely, so your name's in the room when opportunities arise. And most underrated: help your junior staff, because those who mentor and lift others are remembered warmly, recommended widely, and trusted with leadership.

title: Part 10 — Salary progression
paras: Part ten — salary progression. Reputation doesn't only get you hired and promoted; it shows up in your pay. It's one reason two planners with identical experience on paper earn markedly different salaries. The higher earner is usually not more technically able — they're more visible, more commercially valuable, better networked, and better at negotiating. A planner whose name a recruiter knows, and who has options, holds cards the invisible one doesn't. Reputation is, literally, leverage.

The headlines. Changing employer is usually the fastest route to a significant rise, because an external offer is benchmarked to the market while an internal one is benchmarked to your current salary. Negotiate from evidence, and from your whole package, not from need — and don't be afraid to ask; in a candidate's market, employers expect it. Treat counter-offers with caution: they fix the money, but rarely the reasons you looked, and many who accept have moved on within the year. Use a good recruiter, who knows the rate and negotiates at arm's length. And mind the timing — maximum leverage is when you have an offer in hand and they've decided they want you. The full mechanics are in PlanRef's Salaries and Progression guide.

title: Part 11 — Fifty mistakes that damage careers
paras: Part eleven — fifty mistakes that damage careers. I've ranked these roughly, from the most serious — the ones that end candidacies and careers — down to the smaller habits that quietly hold people back. Few make many; most make one or two without realising, which is why they're worth hearing in full.

title: Most serious — these end candidacies and careers
paras: First, the most serious — these end candidacies and careers. One: lying on your C-V, inventing qualifications, dates or experience. Two: misrepresenting your R-T-P-I or professional status, claiming a chartership you don't hold. Three: discriminatory, racist or hateful content online. Four: concealing a professional disciplinary finding — the concealment is worse than the finding. Five: aggressive or abusive public behaviour online, pile-ons and threats.

Six: breaching confidentiality, posting about live cases, clients or employers. Seven: badmouthing former employers. Eight: getting caught in a lie during interview, where one exposed exaggeration collapses your other claims. Nine: extreme political content, conspiracy theories or misinformation — it reads as poor judgement. And ten: offensive 'humour', screenshotted and shared.

title: Serious — these regularly cost jobs and promotions
paras: Next, the serious ones — these regularly cost jobs and promotions. Eleven: no LinkedIn presence at all — in 2026 it reads as hiding. Twelve: a profile that contradicts your C-V. Thirteen: public alcohol, drug or party imagery. Fourteen: an identical generic C-V and cover letter to every role. Fifteen: the wrong company name left in a cover letter. Sixteen: a C-V of duties, not achievements. Seventeen: typos and sloppy formatting. Eighteen: turning up to interview having done no research.

Nineteen: letting your chartership or C-P-D lapse — it closes the door to senior roles. Twenty: accepting a counter-offer for the money alone, when the reasons you left remain. Twenty-one: burning bridges when you resign — planning is a small world. Twenty-two: being slow to reply to a recruiter or employer. Twenty-three: overstating seniority or fabricating a job title. Twenty-four: a careless email address or voicemail. And twenty-five: being rude to junior staff, receptionists or recruiters.

title: Moderate — these quietly hold you back
paras: Then the moderate ones — these quietly hold you back. Twenty-six: never negotiating salary. Twenty-seven: staying invisible — never writing, speaking or contributing. Twenty-eight: never developing a specialism, when specialists are scarce and paid more. Twenty-nine: waiting to be promoted rather than making the case. Thirty: a weak or absent LinkedIn headline. Thirty-one: not tailoring your profile or C-V to where you want to go. Thirty-two: neglecting your network until you need it.

Thirty-three: refusing to help colleagues. Thirty-four: no recommendations on LinkedIn. Thirty-five: ignoring commercial awareness, staying purely technical. Thirty-six: poor interview storytelling, because you never used STAR. Thirty-seven: a bad online-interview setup — dark, looming, glitchy. Thirty-eight: only ever asking about pay and leave. Thirty-nine: never asking for feedback after a rejection. And forty: job-hopping with no narrative of progression.

title: Minor — the habits worth fixing
paras: And finally, the minor ones — the habits worth fixing. Forty-one: an outdated C-V you update only when you need it. Forty-two: a blank LinkedIn banner and a poor photo. Forty-three: connecting with the blank default note. Forty-four: over-formatting the C-V with graphics an A-T-S can't read. Forty-five: listing every task you've ever done, not what mattered.

Forty-six: vague adjectives — 'passionate', 'dynamic', 'hardworking' — with nothing behind them. Forty-seven: never updating your profile after a promotion or big project. Forty-eight: chasing LinkedIn virality over quiet credibility. Forty-nine: forgetting to proofread the email you send the C-V with. And fifty: underselling yourself out of modesty.

title: Part 12 — The six-month career checklist
paras: Part twelve — the six-month career checklist. Careers are built in small, regular steps, not occasional panics. So twice a year — put it in the calendar — spend an hour on this. It's the single most useful habit in the guide.

Your C-V: recent achievements, not duties, still two pages, still A-T-S-clean, still honest. LinkedIn: headline, about and experience current, photo and banner good, a recommendation requested. C-P-D: logged and on track, a knowledge gap identified and a plan to fill it. Membership: subscription paid, chartership progressing or maintained, record clean. Networking: three genuine connections made or renewed, and one event in the diary. Social media: your name searched, personal accounts locked down, nothing public you wouldn't stand behind.

Interview skills: two fresh STAR examples ready to tell. Achievements: written down as they happen, so nothing's forgotten when it counts. Career goals: reviewed — where do you want to be in two years, and is this six months moving you there? Training: one skill or specialism deliberately advanced. Mentoring: helping someone junior, and, whatever your stage, being mentored yourself. And visibility: one thing done to be seen — a comment, an article, a talk, a committee.

That's the whole of it. Do the work. Tell the truth. Be findable. Be generous. And keep the reputation that precedes you one you'd be proud to walk in behind. Do that steadily, and you'll spend far less of your career chasing jobs — the good ones will come looking for you.

title: Sources and notes
paras: A last word on sources. The recruitment figures I've quoted — recruiters on LinkedIn, those screening candidates on social media, those who've rejected someone over a profile — come from recent U-K recruitment surveys, all set out with their sources in the written guide. So is the professional and careers-service guidance behind the C-V, cover-letter, interview and negotiation advice, and the chartership and C-P-D guidance behind the career sections.

Two caveats. The LinkedIn algorithm isn't published, so the posting advice — consistency, comments above likes, dwell time, video — is informed guidance, not gospel, worth re-checking as the platform changes. And the craft advice throughout is drawn from long recruitment experience, offered as judgement. This guide was compiled in 2026 for PlanRef.
